title: Biodegradable and Biocompatible Polymers for 3D-Printed Pharmaceuticals
content: Three-dimensional (3D) printing enables patient-specific pharmaceutical products, local drug-delivery implants, and geometrically programmed release systems. However, printability, biocompatibility, water solubility, and biodegradability represent different material properties and are frequently evaluated using non-equivalent endpoints. This critical review examines original experimental studies, including a 112-record title-coded thematic-mapping corpus (2014–2026). Extrusion-based, powder-based, and vat-photopolymerization technologies are compared alongside synthetic aliphatic polyesters, naturally derived polysaccharides, protein-based hydrogels, and important non-bioresorbable comparators. Studies are organized by oral delivery, transdermal microneedles, wound treatment, ocular and intravaginal products, and implantable depots; an author-curated title-coded thematic network visualizes the selected research categories. A central contribution is a proposed printability–degradation–release–biocompatibility coupling framework that distinguishes measured drug liberation from matrix dissolution, polymer chain scission, mass loss, and verified biological clearance. The framework integrates time-scale ratios, geometry-sensitive transport, and explicitly graded evidence requirements rather than combining unlike studies into an unjustified pooled estimate. Across applications, structural design provides additional control over release, but many reported demonstrations lack matched measurements of polymer degradation, released-species identity, and longer-term biological response. Standardized, application-specific evidence packages are therefore necessary to translate geometrically sophisticated prototypes into dependable pharmaceutical products.
